newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU governments to reveal differences on expansion.
newsitem.headline: EU governments to reveal differences on expansion.

text.p: European Union foreign ministers open five months of horsetrading on Tuesday over the scale and timing of the bloc's expansion to the east.

At a routine meeting in Brussels the ministers will hold a first discussion of a European Commission blueprint unveiled last week which recommended that the bloc open entry talks with five out of 10 eastern bloc applicants early next year.
EU governments, each with their different national interests at stake, have final say over who to invite to join the talks at the EU's December Luxembourg summit. They start out deeply divided.

The European Commission said last week in its Agenda 2000 policy blueprint for the next century that Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Estonia and Slovenia were ready to join Cyprus in EU membership talks.
Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia, Bulgaria and Romania were far from ready and should be held over until later, it said.
French President Jacques Chirac is determined that the 10 eastern applicants should open entry talks at the same time, even though they might join at different dates.
Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen said last week that his country too, reflecting a stand taken by the Nordic bloc as a whole, was committed to talks with all at once.
The Nordic countries want all three Baltic states, formerly part of the Soviet Union, admitted to talks to prevent them slipping back into the Russian sphere of influence.

But the EU's smaller countries like Luxembourg and Belgium want an even smaller expansion than proposed by the Commission to avoid the institutional overhaul which admitting more than five countries would entail.
The EU's June 16-17 Amsterdam Summit failed to agree on the institutional changes necessary for a bloc with up to a dozen new members.

Under the fudge agreed at Amsterdam if the 15-nation EU extends to more than 20 a new intergovernmental conference would have to be held, which would almost certainly challenge the power of the EU's smaller members.

EU foreign ministers will meet at the same time as the bloc's farm ministers, who, with angry farmers breathing down their necks, are expected to take the offensive on Tuesday against the European Commission's latest plans to cut prices.
The proposed price cuts of 10 percent for dairy products and 20 percent for cereals are seen as necessary to prepare the EU for the eastward enlargement.
Diplomats said Germany and France were likely to lead the attack after a presentation by Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler of the proposals.
